story910:
During a time of great famine, when the buffalo had vanished and the people were thin as reeds, two Lakota scouts — young men with sharp eyes and hollow bellies — ventured far from camp in search of game. They found nothing. The plains were empty, the rivers still, the sky a sheet of gray.

As they rested beneath a cottonwood tree, a figure appeared on the horizon. She was beautiful beyond description — a woman dressed in white buckskin that shimmered like fresh snow. She carried a sacred pipe and walked with a grace that made the grass bend beneath her feet.

One scout was overcome with desire. He approached her with lustful intent, thinking only of her beauty. Where he touched her, his flesh turned to bone. His companion, witnessing this horror, knelt in respect.

The woman smiled at the second scout. "I am Ptesáŋ Wiŋ — White Buffalo Calf Woman. I have come to bring your people the sacred pipe, the chanupa, so that they may pray and survive this hard time."

She instructed the scout to prepare the tribe for her arrival. He ran back to camp, his legs carrying him faster than they ever had. The people gathered in a circle, and the White Buffalo Calf Woman walked among them, teaching them the Seven Sacred Rites — the Sun Dance, the vision quest, the sweat lodge, the pipe ceremony, and the rites of passage that would guide their spiritual life.

She gave them the chanupa — a pipe made of red stone carved with the image of a buffalo calf. She showed them how to fill it with the sacred mixture of bark and tobacco, how to offer the smoke to the four directions, how to pray to Wakan Tanka, the Great Mystery.

Before departing, she transformed through four colors — black, then red, then brown, then white — becoming a white buffalo calf who spoke one final promise: "I will return when the people need me most."

The pipe remains the most sacred object in Lakota spirituality. When it is raised, Wakan Tanka listens. When it is smoked, the prayers rise with the smoke to the sky world. And the White Buffalo Calf Woman's promise endures — a light in the darkness, a hope in the famine.
story911:
Iktomi was born fully grown — no childhood, no learning, no gradual awakening. One moment he was nothing, and the next he was a spider with the body of a spider and the cunning of a man. He emerged into the world already knowing its tricks, already planning his schemes.

He was known as the trickster, the weaver of false webs, the maker of predictions that came true in ways no one expected. His stories were told around the fire, each one a warning wrapped in laughter.

In one tale, Iktomi found a pot of fish soup simmering over a fire. It was not his soup. He knew this. He sat down beside it anyway and began to eat. When a visitor arrived — a traveler with hollow cheeks and hopeful eyes — Iktomi devised a trick to keep the soup for himself.

"Let us race," Iktomi said. "The winner takes the soup."

The traveler agreed. Iktomi drew a line in the dirt and told the traveler to run to the cottonwood tree and back. But while the traveler ran, Iktomi ate the soup. When the traveler returned, breathless and victorious, the pot was empty.

The traveler looked at the empty pot. Then he looked at Iktomi. Then he smiled. "You have won the soup," he said. "But you have lost something more valuable — the trust of anyone who hears this story."

Iktomi laughed, but the laughter was hollow, for he knew the traveler was right.

In another tale, Iktomi angered a boulder by insulting its weight and stubbornness. The boulder chased him and crushed him flat. Bats came to help, pecking at the boulder until it cracked open. But the bats' faces were smashed flat in the effort, and Iktomi — ever ungrateful — scattered pebbles that became the stones covering the plains.

Despite his flaws, Iktomi is considered wise. His stories teach moral lessons about generosity, respect, and the consequences of selfishness. He is the trickster who reveals truth through deception, who teaches wisdom through folly.
story912:
Unhcegila was a gigantic serpent monster who wreaked havoc upon the land. She was older than the hills, older than the rivers, older than the memory of the people. Her body stretched across entire valleys, and her scales were harder than stone.

She devoured anyone who stumbled upon her path — hunters, women, children. No weapon could pierce her hide. No arrow could find her heart. She was, it seemed, invincible.

But Unhcegila had a weakness. In the seventh spot on her head, there was a red crystal — her heart, glowing like an ember. Whoever possessed this crystal would gain great power.

In one version of the story, a warrior from the Bear Clan was guided by a Weasel spirit to the serpent's lair. The warrior was brave but small, and he knew he could not fight Unhcegila directly. So he devised a plan.

He allowed himself to be devoured. The serpent swallowed him whole, and for a moment the warrior thought he would die. But inside the serpent's belly, he found the bones of those who had been taken before him. He also found the red crystal, pulsing with power.

The warrior cut his way out of the serpent's belly, freeing the other victims as he went. When he emerged, he held the crystal high. Unhcegila, weakened by the loss of her heart, fell to the ground and died.

In another version, two brothers — one blind — killed the serpent with arrows from a medicine woman. The blind brother could not see the serpent, but his brother guided his aim, and the arrows found their mark.

In a third version, Unhcegila emerged from primordial waters, only to be struck down by Wakinyan the Thunderbird, whose lightning shattered her heart and scattered her bones across the Badlands.

The story teaches that even the most terrifying adversaries have vulnerabilities, and that courage, observation, and cunning can overcome seemingly insurmountable threats.
story913:
In the beginning there was only Inyan — Rock — and the omnipresent spirit Wakan Tanka, the Great Mystery, and the darkness Han. Nothing else existed. No earth, no sky, no beings of any kind.

Inyan wished to exercise his powers of compassion. He wanted to create something — anything — that would know the warmth of his spirit and the strength of his body. So he created Maka — Earth — from himself, tearing pieces of his own being and shaping them into the land.

But the creation cost him dearly. His blood — the red ochre that gives rock its color — flowed into the earth, becoming water. As his blood flowed, Inyan shriveled and lost his powers. The rock that had once been vast and mighty became small and hard, embedded in the earth it had created.

The water gave birth to Skan — the Sky — who became the supreme judge. Skan looked down at the world below and saw Maka, the earth, shivering in the cold and darkness. Maka complained of her suffering — she was alone, she was cold, she had no light.

Inyan, even in his weakened state, heard her complaint. He created Anpo the Dawn — a being of soft pink and gold who walked across the sky each morning, bringing the first hint of light. And later he created Wi the Sun — the full blazing light that turned the world from gray to green.

But Maka tried to separate from Inyan. She wanted to be free of the rock that had created her, to float in the water without weight or burden. Skan ruled that rock and soil must remain bound together — that Inyan and Maka could never be fully separated.

This is why rocks are embedded in the earth, why boulders sit in the middle of fields and stones line the riverbeds. Inyan cannot leave Maka, and Maka cannot shed Inyan. They are bound together by Skan's judgment, by the sacrifice of creation, by the love that Inyan gave when he tore himself apart to make the world.

The story teaches the Lakota understanding that creation requires sacrifice, that love costs something, and that the bonds between beings — even unwilling ones — are sacred.
story914:
Wakinyan — the Thunderbird — is the great sky spirit of Lakota mythology, a being of such power that even the other spirits treat him with caution. His body is massive, spanning the width of the sky when his wings are spread. His feathers are red and gold, and his eyes flash with the lightning that is his weapon and his voice.

When Wakinyan flaps his wings, thunderclaps shake the earth. When he opens his eyes, lightning bolts split the sky. When he speaks, his voice is the rumble that precedes the storm.

Wakinyan is the protector of the Lakota people against chaos and disorder. He is the eternal enemy of the great water serpents — Unhcegila and her kind — who lurk in the depths of lakes and rivers, waiting to devour the unwary.

When Unhcegila emerged from the primordial waters to flood the land, it was Wakinyan who rose to meet her. He flapped his wings to dry the earth, his feathers sending waves of heat across the plains. He shot lightning at the serpent's heart, the red crystal that was her weakness.

The battle was terrible. The sky turned black with Wakinyan's wings. The earth shook with Unhcegila's thrashing. Lightning and water clashed in a storm that lasted four days and four nights.

Finally, Wakinyan's lightning struck the crystal. The serpent's heart shattered, and she fell. Her body became the Badlands — the eroded, twisted landscape that the Lakota call Makhóšiča, the Bad Lands, where her bones still jut from the earth like fingers reaching for the sky.

Wakinyan is associated with the west direction, where storms come from. He is honored with tobacco offerings, and his rumbling voice is heard whenever he pursues evil spirits across the sky. The Lakota say that when thunder rolls, Wakinyan is speaking — warning the monsters below that the Thunderbird is watching, that the protector of the people is on patrol.
story915:
The four-legged animals and the two-legged birds had been arguing for as long as anyone could remember. The animals said they were stronger and deserved to eat the birds. The birds said they were swifter and deserved to eat the animals. Neither side would yield.

Ksapela the Wise One — a being older than the argument itself — proposed a solution. "Let there be a race," she said. "The winner eats the loser."

Representing the four-leggeds was the buffalo — massive, powerful, his hooves cracking the earth with each step. Representing the two-leggeds was the magpie — small, sharp-eyed, with wings that could carry him faster than any four-legged could run.

The race began at dawn. The buffalo surged forward, his massive body cutting through the prairie grass like a ship through water. The magpie flew beside him, his wings beating steadily.

As the race progressed, various animals helped their champion. The rabbit dug a hole in the buffalo's path, giving him a smooth route. The fox ran alongside, barking encouragement. The magpie had no helpers — he relied on his own wings.

The buffalo was winning. He was so close to the finish line that he could taste victory. But the magpie, watching from above, saw his chance. He dove and landed on the buffalo's back. The buffalo didn't notice — the magpie was so light.

At the last moment, just before the buffalo crossed the finish line, the magpie launched himself into the air and flew ahead. He landed on the finish line first.

The Great Spirit declared the race a draw. Neither side had clearly won. But the decree established the rules that would govern the relationship between animals and birds forever: henceforth, the two-leggeds would hunt the four-leggeds, but they must always show respect for their sacrifice.

The magpie still wears the black and white feathers he wore during the race. The buffalo still runs across the plains, his great body a reminder of the race that determined the fate of all living things.
story916:
The Lakota believe the soul does not die with the body. When a person breathes their last, the soul rises from the chest like a bird taking flight, and it begins its journey to the happy hunting ground — a realm that resembles the living world but with better weather, more plentiful animals, and easier hunting.

Some traditions say the soul travels along the Sky-Road — the Milky Way, that river of light that stretches across the night sky. The road is well-marked, lined with the souls of those who came before, each one a star in the constellation of the ancestors.

At the entrance to the happy hunting ground, the deceased must present proper tattoos to Hihankara — the Owl-Maker, a spirit who guards the gate. The tattoos are not decorative but identifying — they mark the soul as belonging to the Lakota people, carrying the symbols of their clans and their achievements.

Those with correct tattoos are admitted. Those without are pushed back to Earth to wander as restless ghosts, unable to find peace because they failed to prepare for the journey.

The dead may also travel along the Spirit Path — another name for the Milky Way — to reach their final resting place among the stars. The Spirit Path is not merely a road but a living thing, growing wider with each soul that walks it, brighter with each star that joins.

The happy hunting ground is not merely a reward but a continuation. The souls of the dead hunt, pray, and live much as they did on earth — but without pain, without hunger, without the winter that bites and the summer that scorches. They are whole again, reunited with those they loved, waiting for the day when the living join them.

The Lakota say that when you look up at the Milky Way, you are looking at the road the dead have walked. And when a new star appears, a soul has found its way home.
